title: A winter morning at Panchavati
hookLine: a cold dawn by the river, a brother says one sentence too many, and Rama shows how Hindus are taught to speak
carry: satyam, priyam: speak what's true, and kindly

lines: A WALK TO THE RIVER AT DAWN.
cards: Time passes at Panchavati, and the season turns to hemanta, early winter. One morning before sunrise, the three of them walk down to the Godavari to bathe.
Lakshmana carries the water pot, and he talks, the way people do on cold walks. Mist over the fields. The sun weak and far away.
Water so cold, he says, that even the elephants touch it with their trunks and pull back.

teach.b: Then Lakshmana's mind goes home. Right now, he says, Bharata is probably walking down to the Sarayu in this same cold.
He could live in a palace; instead he sleeps on the ground and keeps an ascetic's vows, out of love for you. Then he adds one sentence too many.

teach.h: HOW COULD SHE HAVE SUCH A SON?
teach.b: How could a mother like Kaikeyi have a son like Bharata? Rama stops him. Don't speak badly of our middle mother, he says.
Speak only of Bharata. And he says how much he misses him; Bharata's kind words come back to him like nectar. Rama lost a kingdom to Kaikeyi's wish, and he's the one who won't allow the bitterness.
He doesn't say she was right. He just won't let the talk turn sour.
Many Hindu families know an old Sanskrit saying for this: satyam bruyat, priyam bruyat. Speak what's true, speak what's kind. Don't speak a truth to wound, and don't speak a sweet lie.
Rama keeps both halves. Now the week. Viradha: the self was never the curse.
Sharabhanga: darshan, worth more than heaven. The sages: refuge, and Rama's yes. Sita: ahimsa, and the protector's bow.
Panchavati: Rama's family on the altar, and a cold morning where blame stops at the door. This quiet is about to end.

how: Some Hindu teachers cite Rama's refusal to let Lakshmana speak ill of Kaikeyi as an example of restraint in speech within a family. The saying satyam bruyat, priyam bruyat comes from the Manusmriti and is widely quoted on its own.

o: the cold season, when even elephants shy from the water
the town where Bharata sleeps on the ground for Rama
the riverside home where Rama won't let Kaikeyi be blamed

games.q: a winter morning — tap the pairs.
p: speak what's true, and what's kind
bathing in the Sarayu in the same cold

s: Lakshmana criticizes Kaikeyi on the walk to the river
he wonders how she could have a son like Bharata.
Rama agrees that Kaikeyi was cruel
he tells Lakshmana not to speak badly of their middle mother.
satyam bruyat, priyam bruyat means only say nice things, true or not
it means speak the truth, kindly, and never a sweet lie. Rama doesn't defend Kaikeyi; he refuses the bitterness.

games.q: you're Rama. your brother, on a cold walk, says something bitter about the stepmother who exiled you. what do you do?
o: stop him, and talk about Bharata instead.
games.why: Rama says: don't speak badly of our middle mother. speak only of Bharata. true and kind at once: satyam, priyam.

practice: Feel the breath come in cool through the nose and leave warm. Think of someone you've been tempted to complain about, then someone connected to them whom you love or admire.
If you pray, ask, as many Hindus do, for speech that's true and kind today. If you don't, rest your attention on the good one, breathing in cool and out warm.

wordCard.voice: Panchavati. A winter dawn by the Godavari, where Rama tells Lakshmana: don't speak badly of our middle mother. Speak of Bharata.

orig.note: Sanskrit hemanta: the early-winter season, one of the traditional seasons of the Indian year.

carryVoice: Your line: satyam, priyam: speak what's true, and kindly. Tomorrow, the quiet breaks. A week deeper into the forest, done.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Aranya Kanda 16 (the winter morning; Lakshmana on Bharata and Kaikeyi; Rama's reply)
Manusmriti 4.138 (speak what is true and pleasant; not an unpleasant truth, nor a pleasant falsehood; paraphrased)
